content: Certainly. Adverse Reactions and Side Effects: Altered taste perception occurs in 3-7% of adults. Diarrhea is reported in 3-6% of cases. Nausea affects 3-6% of adults. Vomiting occurs in 1% of adults and 6% of children. Elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels are observed in 4% of cases. Abdominal pain is reported in 2% of adults and 3% of children. Rash is seen in 3% of children. Dyspepsia (indigestion) occurs in 2% of cases. Heartburn affects 2% of adults. Headache is reported in 2% of cases. Elevated prothrombin time (PT) is observed in 1% of cases. Rare but Serious Reactions: Anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction, has been reported. Anorexia (loss of appetite) and anxiety may occur. Clostridium difficile-associated colitis, a severe intestinal condition, has been documented. Dizziness and dyspnea (difficulty breathing) are possible. Elevated liver function tests, glossitis (inflammation of the tongue), and hallucinations have been observed. Hepatic dysfunction, including hepatitis and jaundice, may occur. Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) has been reported, particularly in patients taking oral hypoglycemic agents or insulin. Increased levels of alkaline phosphatase, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), bilirubin, and serum creatinine have been noted. Leukopenia (low white blood cell count) and neutropenia (low neutrophil count) have been reported. Pancreatitis and psychosis are rare but possible. QT interval prolongation, which can lead to arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes, has been associated with this medication. Seizures and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, a severe skin reaction, have been documented. Thrombocytopenia (low platelet count) and agranulocytosis (severe reduction in white blood cells) are potential risks. System-Specific Disorders: Cardiac Disorders: Torsades de pointes, ventricular tachycardia, and ventricular arrhythmias have been reported. Ear and Labyrinth Disorders: Reversible deafness, primarily in elderly women, has been observed. Gastrointestinal Disorders: Acute pancreatitis, tongue discoloration, and tooth discoloration have been noted. Hepatobiliary Disorders: Hepatic failure and hepatocellular jaundice have been reported. Immune System Disorders: Anaphylactic reactions and angioedema (swelling) may occur. Infections: Pseudomembranous colitis has been associated with this medication. Investigations: Prolonged prothrombin time, decreased white blood cell count, and increased international normalized ratio (INR) have been observed. Abnormal urine color has been linked to hepatic failure. Metabolism and Nutrition Disorders: Hypoglycemia has been reported, especially in patients on concurrent hypoglycemic therapy. Musculoskeletal Disorders: Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown) have been reported, particularly when used with statins, fibrates, colchicine, or allopurinol. Nervous System Disorders: Convulsions, ageusia (loss of taste), parosmia (distorted smell), anosmia (loss of smell), and paresthesia (tingling sensations) have been documented. Psychiatric Disorders: Psychotic disorders, confusion, depersonalization, depression, disorientation, manic behavior, hallucinations, abnormal behavior, and vivid dreams have been reported. Renal and Urinary Disorders: Interstitial nephritis and renal failure have been observed. Skin Disorders: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), Henoch-Schönlein purpura, and acne have been reported. Vascular Disorders: Hemorrhage has been documented. Warnings and Precautions: Colchicine Toxicity: Fatal cases of colchicine toxicity have been reported when clarithromycin was co-administered with colchicine, particularly in elderly patients or those with renal insufficiency. Superinfections: Prolonged use may result in fungal or bacterial superinfections. HIV Patients: Increased mortality has been observed in HIV patients with Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) treated with doses exceeding the recommended maximum. Resistance to clarithromycin has been noted when used for prophylaxis or treatment of MAC infections. Hypersensitivity Reactions: Severe hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and DRESS syndrome, require immediate discontinuation. QT Prolongation: Avoid use in patients with ongoing proarrhythmic conditions (e.g., uncorrected hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia, significant bradycardia). Patients aged 65 years or older may be more susceptible to drug-induced QT prolongation. Hepatic Dysfunction: Cases of severe hepatic dysfunction, including hepatitis and jaundice, have been reported. Discontinue immediately if symptoms of hepatitis (e.g., anorexia, jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, tender abdomen) occur. Coronary Heart Disease: Increased morbidity has been observed in patients with coronary heart disease who received a two-week course of clarithromycin. Clostridium difficile-Associated Diarrhea: This condition may occur during or after treatment. Pregnancy: Use during pregnancy is not recommended unless no alternative therapy is available. Patients should be informed of potential risks to the fetus. Breastfeeding: Clarithromycin and its active metabolite are present in human milk at low levels. Adverse effects on breastfed infants (e.g., rash, diarrhea, loss of appetite, somnolence) have been reported. Pharmacokinetics: Clarithromycin is a semisynthetic macrolide antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit. It is highly stable in gastric acid, unlike erythromycin. Food delays absorption but does not affect its extent. Bioavailability is approximately 50%. Peak plasma time is 2-3 hours for immediate release and 5-8 hours for extended release. It is widely distributed in body tissues except for the central nervous system. Protein binding is 42-50%. It is partially metabolized by CYP3A4, with an active metabolite, 14-OH clarithromycin. The half-life is 3-7 hours for immediate release and 5-9 hours for the active metabolite. Excretion occurs primarily via urine (30-55%). Storage and Administration: Store tablets at controlled room temperature (20-25°C or 68-77°F). Reconstituted granules should be shaken well before each use. Tablets or granules can be taken with or without food. Important Notes: This medication is prescribed for your current condition only. Do not stop taking the medication without consulting your doctor. If a dose is missed, take it as soon as you remember unless it is near the time for the next dose. Properly discard expired or unused medication.
